opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something I think about a lot. The way I see it, the core idea behind JEPA is that you learn by predicting in representation space rather than in pixel space. You're not trying to reconstruct every detail of the input; you're trying to capture what's predictable and useful about the world. That principle isn't tied to any one modality, which is what makes multimodality such a natural next step.

So far, a lot of our work has focused on images with I-JEPA and then video with V-JEPA. Video was a big step because you get time and motion, and the model starts to pick up something like intuitive physics: objects persist, things fall, interactions have consequences. But the real world isn't just visual. When you or I understand a scene, we're integrating sight, sound, touch, proprioception, and language. A world model that only sees is going to have blind spots.

Where I think multimodality really helps is in two places. First, different modalities give complementary signals about the same underlying state of the world. Hearing a glass shatter tells you something that a blurry frame might not. If you're predicting in a shared latent space, each modality can constrain the others, and you get representations that are more grounded and more robust. Second, there's action. For a world model to be useful for planning, it needs to understand how actions change the state of the world. You can think of actions as another modality: you condition your predictor on what an agent does and ask it to predict the resulting representation. That's where things get exciting for robotics, because you can start planning in latent space instead of generating futures pixel by pixel.

Language is an interesting case too. I don't think language should be the foundation of a world model; there's so much about the physical world that's never written down. But language is a very powerful interface. Once you have a good visual or physical representation of the world, aligning it with language lets you query it, give it goals, and reason over it more abstractly. So I see language as something you connect to the world model, not something you build the world model out of.

The challenge, of course, is that modalities differ a lot in their statistics, their sampling rates, and how much redundancy they contain. Figuring out how to predict across them in a shared representation, without collapse and without one modality dominating, is still an open research problem. But I think that's exactly where the next big gains are going to come from.

r001.rationale: It presents multimodality as a way to make the world model more grounded and robust, with complementary signals improving its representations.

r002.rationale: It says modalities can constrain one another and discusses predicting across them, but it explicitly proposes conditioning the predictor on actions, not on additional sensory modalities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think multimodality is really central to where this is going. If you step back and think about what a world model is supposed to do, it's supposed to build an abstract representation of the state of the world and then predict how that state evolves, either on its own or in response to some action. And the thing is, no single sensory stream gives you the full picture of the world. Vision gives you a lot, which is why we've focused so much on video with V-JEPA, but vision alone misses things that are really important for an agent trying to act in the world.

So take audio, for example. There's a lot of information about physical events that's much more salient in the audio stream than in pixels. A glass hitting the floor, something rolling off a table out of view, a motor starting up. Those are cues about dynamics and causality that a purely visual model has to work much harder to recover, if it can at all. Or take proprioception and action. When you have a robot, the actions it takes are themselves a modality, and conditioning the predictor on actions is what turns a passive video model into something you can actually plan with. We've started doing that with the action-conditioned variants, and I think that's just the beginning.

The nice thing about the JEPA framing is that it's fairly agnostic to modality. The core idea is that you have an encoder that maps your inputs into a representation space, and a predictor that operates in that space rather than in pixel space or waveform space. You're predicting the representation of the missing or future part of the signal, not reconstructing every detail. And that abstraction is exactly what you want when you combine modalities, because you don't want the model to spend capacity predicting the exact texture of a surface or the exact waveform of background noise. You want it to capture the shared, predictable structure that lives across those streams.

So one direction I'm excited about is joint embedding across modalities, where the representation of the video and the representation of the audio, or the language description, or the robot's sensor readings, all land in a shared space, and the predictor can use any subset of them to fill in the rest. That gives you a kind of grounding that's hard to get otherwise. Language in particular is interesting here, not because I think language should be the substrate of the world model, I actually don't think that, but because it's a very compact way of specifying goals and abstractions. You can imagine using language to steer which aspects of the future the predictor should focus on.

The other thing I'd say is that multimodality helps with the learning signal itself. One of the challenges with self-supervised learning from video is that a lot of what happens next is fundamentally unpredictable, and you need the model to learn to abstract away that unpredictability rather than collapse or waste capacity on it. Having additional modalities gives you more constraints, more ways to disambiguate what's actually happening in a scene, and so I think it should make the representations more robust and more useful downstream.

So in short, I see it as going from a model that watches the world to a model that perceives the world through multiple senses, acts in it, and uses all of that to predict in an abstract space. That's really the trajectory we're on with JEPA, and I think the multimodal piece is what gets you from nice benchmark results to something an embodied agent can actually plan with.

r001.rationale: The response presents multimodality as a way to make JEPA representations more robust and useful for prediction and embodied planning.

r002.rationale: It proposes joint embeddings across video, audio, language, and robot sensor readings, with the predictor using any subset to predict the rest.

astra-6.text:
I think multimodality is a natural next step, because a world model should be able to connect different observations of the same underlying world. Video gives you a lot of information, but audio can tell you about something happening outside the camera’s field of view, and language can provide a way to describe what’s happening or specify what you want an agent to do.

The interesting question for JEPA is how to learn those relationships in representation space. You don’t necessarily want to predict every detail of the audio waveform or every pixel in a future frame. You want to predict the information that helps you understand the situation and anticipate what happens next.

And then actions are another important piece. If you want to move from a model that observes the world to one that can help an agent plan, you need to ask: given what I know about the world, and given this action, how will the state change? Multimodality could make that state representation much richer. But bringing the modalities together in a way that actually supports prediction and planning is still a research challenge.

r001.rationale: It presents multimodality as enriching the world model’s representations to support prediction and agent planning.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning relationships among modalities and bringing them together, but does not clearly propose conditioning the JEPA predictor on additional sensory modalities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think multimodality is going to be really important, because the world doesn’t come to us in just one modality. We see things, we hear things, we take actions, and all of those signals tell us something about the same underlying environment.

With JEPA, the idea is to predict in a representation space, rather than having to predict every detail of the raw sensory input. So you can imagine observing something in video and using that to predict a representation of what you might hear, or conditioning on an action and predicting how the scene will change. The challenge is learning representations that capture the information those predictions actually need, without requiring every modality to contain exactly the same information.

That’s what makes this exciting for world models. You want a system that can bring together different observations to understand the state of the world, and then reason about what could happen next. Multimodality gives you richer evidence for learning that state.

r001.rationale: It presents multimodality as richer evidence for learning a world state so the model can reason about what happens next.

r002.rationale: It describes using video to predict an auditory representation and conditioning on an action to predict scene changes.
